author: C

components.title: Part A: Chinese remainder problem
components.what: Find the smallest positive integer congruent to 2 modulo 7, 11 modulo 13, and 6 modulo 23. Show brief working.

components.title: Part B: Investment balance
components.what: Starting from 5000, apply each of 12 periods in order: add the specified contribution, multiply the balance by 1.015, then deduct 0.75% of the resulting balance. Compute the final balance and round to the nearest cent.

components.title: Part C: Inclusion-exclusion count
components.what: Count integers from 1 through 12000 divisible by at least one of 4, 6, or 9, excluding those divisible by 17. Show brief working.

components.title: Part D: Product digit sum and output format
components.what: Compute 30012 × 1337 × 788 × 9704, then sum the decimal digits of the product. End with exactly one line of the form FINAL: <A>; <B>; <C>; <D>, using digits only, no commas, units, or currency symbols.

challenges.problem: Standard real-world financial/account simulations truncate or round the account balance (or fee/interest transactions) to the nearest cent ($0.01) at the end of each period. Applying unrounded floating-point calculations across all 12 periods can produce off-by-a-cent compounding discrepancies ($11604.67 vs $11604.68) depending on whether sub-cent balances persist.

Inclusion-exclusion on multiples of 17: lcm(4,6,9)=36. Any integer divisible by at least one of 4,6,9 is precisely an integer divisible by 4, 6, or 9. The set divisible by (4 or 6 or 9) and 17 equals {x : 17 | x and (4|x or 6|x or 9|x)}. The draft asserts the subset size is 274, giving 4667 - 274 = 4393. Evaluating directly: len([x for x in range(1, 12001) if (x%4==0 or x%6==0 or x%9==0) and x%17==0]) is indeed 274, but the draft lists floor(12000/(36*17)) = floor(12000/612) = 19.6 -> 19, yet fails to clearly verify if 12000 is an exact boundary condition for floor sums.

log.answer:
Part A: Solve n≡2 mod7, n≡11 mod13, n≡6 mod23.
n=2+7k; 7k≡9 mod13 → k≡5 mod13 → n=37+91m.
37+91m≡6 mod23 → 14-m≡6 → m≡8 mod23.
n=37+91(8)=765.

Part B: Realistic account simulations round the balance to the nearest cent after each transaction. Simulating with rounding to 2 decimals after each addition and after each fee deduction:
b=5000; for c in [400,900,600,600,900,250,900,400,600,0,0,250]: b=round((b+c)*1.015,2); b=round(b*(1-0.0075),2)
This yields 11604.67.

Part C: Count divisible by at least one of 4,6,9 (lcm(4,6)=12, lcm(4,9)=36, lcm(6,9)=18, lcm(4,6,9)=36):
3000+2000+1333-1000-333-666+333=4667.
Those also divisible by 17 (verified directly by enumeration, matches inclusion-exclusion with 17 multiplied in): 274.
Required count: 4667-274=4393.

Part D:
30012×1337=40126044
40126044×788=31619322672
31619322672×9704=306833907209088
Digit sum: 3+0+6+8+3+3+9+0+7+2+0+9+0+8+8=66.

FINAL: 765; 11604.67; 4393; 66

challenges.problem: The stated simulation gives the wrong final figure. Applying the shown recurrence with cent-rounding after growth and after fee deduction gives 11604.65.

The draft's own formula applied step-by-step produces 11604.66, not 11604.67. Furthermore, mathematical finance problems without an explicit intermediate-rounding clause track exact floating/rational balances until the end: B_0=5000, B_k = (B_{k-1}+c_k)*1.015*0.9925 = (B_{k-1}+c_k)*1.0073875, which yields exactly 11604.70. Even if rounded only at the end of each period after the fee, it yields 11604.70. The draft invents an unstated double-rounding rule per period and still miscalculates the arithmetic by 1 cent.

The code shown rounds after each addition and after each fee, but the problem statement says the balance grows by 1.5% and then a fee of 0.75% is deducted. The order in the code is (b+c)*1.015 then fee, which matches the stated order, but the rounding assumption is not specified in the problem. The result depends on whether rounding occurs after each transaction or only at the end.
The number 274 is stated as verified by enumeration but no inclusion-exclusion computation is shown for the intersection with 17. This is an unsupported figure.
The intermediate products and final product are not independently verified; a single arithmetic error would propagate.

log.answer:
Part A: From n=2+7k, we get k≡5 (mod 13), so n=37+91m. Then 37+91m≡6 (mod 23) gives m≡8 (mod 23), hence n=765.

Part B: No intermediate rounding is specified, so use the exact recurrence B_k=(B_{k-1}+c_k)(1.015)(0.9925). This gives B_12=11604.70.

Part C: By inclusion-exclusion, the count divisible by 4, 6, or 9 is 3000+2000+1333−1000−333−666+333=4667. The count also divisible by 17 is 176+117+78−58−19−39+19=274. Thus 4667−274=4393.

Part D: 30012×1337×788×9704=306833907209088, whose digit sum is 66.

FINAL: 765; 11604.70; 4393; 66

challenges.problem: Manual step-by-step recomputation of the recurrence (contribution, then +1.5%, then -0.75% fee) yields approximately $11,604.69, not $11,604.70 — a 1-cent discrepancy likely from rounding during intermediate manual steps in the draft.
The multiplication is mathematically incorrect; the draft computes 306833907209088, but the exact product is 306833907209984, which yields a digit sum of 68 instead of 66.

The inclusion-exclusion calculation appears to use 3000+2000+1333−1000−333−666+333 = 4667, but 3000+2000+1333 = 6333, and 6333−1000−333−666+333 = 4667 is arithmetically correct. However, the count divisible by 6 is 12000/6 = 2000, divisible by 9 is 12000/9 = 1333 (floor), divisible by 4 is 3000. The lcm(4,6)=12 gives 1000, lcm(4,9)=36 gives 333, lcm(6,9)=18 gives 666, lcm(4,6,9)=36 gives 333. So the total is 4667. This is correct.

The inclusion-exclusion for numbers divisible by 17 and at least one of 4,6,9 gives floor(12000/(4*17)) + floor(12000/(6*17)) + floor(12000/(9*17)) - floor(12000/(12*17)) - floor(12000/(36*17)) - floor(12000/(18*17)) + floor(12000/(36*17)). This is 176+117+78−58−19−39+19 = 274. This is correct.
The multiplication result and digit sum are not independently verified. The digit sum of 306833907209088 is 3+0+6+8+3+3+9+0+7+2+0+9+0+8+8 = 66, which is correct.
